claims.text: Oxidation resistance and material integrity in high-temperature multiprincipal-element alloys derive from a dynamic near-surface transformation.
The near-surface transformation produces an ultra-nanocrystalline layer.
The transformed near-surface layer is an amorphous precursor to a protective oxide scale.
CoCrFeMnNi can be a single-phase high-entropy alloy.
The initial CoCrFeMnNi material can be coarse-grained.
Mechanical pre-straining can promote near-surface dynamic amorphization in CoCrFeMnNi.
Thermal cycling can promote near-surface dynamic amorphization in CoCrFeMnNi.
Under high-temperature oxidizing conditions, stress and thermal energy drive dynamic surface amorphization.
The nanostructured or amorphous surface layer accelerates nucleation and growth of a uniform, adherent oxide scale.
The resulting oxide scale limits oxygen ingress.
Multiprincipal elements inherently stabilize grain boundaries in a way that contributes to oxidation resistance and mechanical integrity.
Pre-conditioned samples will oxidize more slowly than unconditioned coarse-grained controls.
Pre-conditioned samples will form a thinner, more uniform, and more adherent oxide scale than controls.
Pre-conditioned samples will retain mechanical properties better and show less oxidation-induced embrittlement than controls.
Unconditioned coarse-grained specimens will form less coherent or patchy oxide scales.
Less coherent or patchy oxide scales will cause faster oxidation penetration and greater material degradation.
The proposed behavior should hold over approximately 800–1100 degrees Celsius.
At substantially lower or higher temperatures, other mechanisms may dominate or dynamic amorphization may be suppressed or overwhelmed by degradation.

contradictions.description: The transformed layer is described interchangeably as ultra-nanocrystalline and amorphous. These are distinct structural states, and the hypothesis does not specify whether the mediator is crystalline, amorphous, or a sequential transition between them.
